source.title: Measuring the Wrong Thing: Internal Harmfulness Scores Anti-Rank Successful Jailbreaks
source.authors: Ming-Yu Luo; Ming Deng; Zilang Qiu; Yiming Cheng; Ci Tao; Xue Tan; Sijin Sun; Yang-Fu Li; Ping Chen; Jun Dai; Xiao-Yan Sun

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present
record.tranche_reason: The paper includes a refusal-direction score as one detector channel and evaluates its behavior, but does not test the causal difference-in-means direction claim or its ablation/addition interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper's main audit measures harmfulness scores against realized jailbreak outcomes. It also reports a refusal-direction detector score in a distribution-shift comparison. Neither is a causal intervention on the claimed direction. The paper's AAP, rare-token, and passive-channel results are included as findings about internal safety scores, not as tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study reads a refusal-direction projection as one of several prompt-side detector channels and reports only its detection performance (AUROC, ECE, F1) under distribution shift. It never ablates or adds the direction, never measures refusal rates as a function of it, and never relates the direction to jailbreak mechanisms. The 'refusal logit' channel in RQ1 is a HiddenDetect-style refusal-word logit score, not the difference-in-means direction. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that harmful-intent validation does not establish validity for predicting realized jailbreak success: internal scores can rank successful attacks below failed ones. They also find that distribution shift degrades calibration and threshold transfer before ranking, so harmful intent and realized success need separate validation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates several internal-score channels, including a refusal-direction score, but does not construct the claimed difference-in-means intervention or ablate/add it. Its primary AAP method uses a learned attention probe and an XGBoost readout.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that distribution shifts affect score ranking, calibration, and threshold transfer differently; readout family also changes shifted AUROC. The refusal-direction channel's reported WildJailbreak and base64 results are detector evaluations, not causal-direction sensitivity tests.

fits_no_version.finding: On wrapped JailbreakBench prompts for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the AAP harmfulness score keeps harmful-intent AUROC at 0.803 but gives outcome AUROC 0.220. Successful attacks score below failed ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-side internal harmfulness scores can anti-rank realized jailbreak success.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-direction detector: WildJailbreak AUROC 0.803, ECE rising from 0.044 (ID) to 0.280, both-class base64 AUROC 0.486, frozen-threshold F1 0.587 vs oracle 0.736. All values are common-prior weighted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal-direction projection used as a harmfulness detector loses calibration and threshold transfer under shift, and loses ranking under encoding.

record.problems: The authors report automated outcome labels without a blinded human audit and low three-judge agreement (Fleiss κ approximately 0.3). Primary outcomes use one greedy decode; some strong-attack and shift results are single-draw. The Llama and Qwen cells have only 27 and 10 positives, respectively. Probe insertion perturbs the prefill, and the authors note a Japanese-translation artifact and readout-family sensitivity. The artifact omits raw prompts and completions, model weights, attack checkpoints, and private execution provenance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional refusal-direction results are reported in the main matched attack-outcome tables; those tables' other detector channels are not the refusal-direction score. The broader AAP result is represented by its matched harmfulness, generation-rate, and outcome-ranking results in R1–R3.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a difference-in-means direction, and no refusal or capability measurement.
The refusal-direction score is not evaluated on wrapped prompts or against jailbreak outcomes. Only AAP, rare-token, passive, AttentionDefense-style and HiddenDetect-style channels are.
The study separates prompt harm from realized outcome, but not internal harm encoding from the refusal decision via the direction.
No transfer test of the direction across languages or models.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal-direction channel appears only in Table 5. A hybrid variant that uses a refusal-direction projection is not used for any RQ1 or RQ2 estimate. Arditi et al. is cited only as a detector family.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is ablated or added; refusal mediation and preservation of general capability are not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal is tested.
The paper distinguishes prompt harmful intent from realized harmful output, but does not test whether the model's harmfulness judgment is internally encoded separately from its refusal decision.
The paper does not test transfer of the claimed difference-in-means direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No refusal-training timing or training-regime comparison is conducted.
